posts.title: On the Matters of Grudge and Forgiveness
posts.html:
In all honesty, when I was a kid I was a really grudge bearing human. You betrayed me during a board game? Grudge. You did not keep your promise? Grudge. You fought with me over something minor? Grudge. You get the point. This kind of continued till I was in college. By then I had learned to forgive people for the sake of social norms, or at least act like I did, but I always kept the spite. I could be talking normally with someone while still remembering that one thing they did months ago.

Eventually, all that spite started catching up to me through my health. Who knew keeping a lurking unresolved feeling inside could harm you, right? I also saw some of my friendships ending because of it, and so forth. I was carrying old anger into new situations and then wondering why everything felt so heavy. It was detrimental, in all honesty.

Fortunately, after my breakup I started watching Vinland Saga. I really loved the kid and teen version of Thorfinn, very relatable in my opinion at that time. The kid had his father killed right in front of him, so who would not be vengeful? The show shows his transformation from a curious child into a vengeful beast who knows and seeks nothing except avenging his father. He follows Askeladd for years and keeps fighting for another chance at giving him what Thorfinn believes would be a proper warrior’s defeat.

Spoiler alert. In the end, Askeladd dies by Canute’s hand before Thorfinn can defeat him. Thorfinn never gets the death for which he trained and waited all those years. As Askeladd is dying, he looks at Thorfinn and asks him: “What are you going to do now? How do you intend to live your life... after I’m gone?”

The whole point of his vengeance dies right there. His entire existence is shattered because he never thought about any other life aside from this one goal. He had spent so many years thinking about how Askeladd would die that he never thought about how he himself would live after that. So what I learned was that vengeance is a fool’s game and a grudge does nothing for anyone in the long term. It makes you bitter and slowly sucks everything out of you.

The above paragraph is good in theory, but when it is your turn to get betrayed or let down, you will not reason that easily with the situation. But why is it so hard to forgive? Well, I guess a part of you finds forgiveness itself to be self betrayal. The mind also somehow mixes forgiving with forgetting. It starts feeling like if you forgive them, you also have to act as if nothing happened, and that itself feels like a betrayal. That is not what I mean by forgiveness though.

It is, on the contrary, an active and dynamic decision to let go of the anger whenever it comes back, through whatever ways a person has figured out for themselves. It sure feels really tough, especially when the anger feels justified. But one thing we all forget from time to time is that forgiveness is something we do for ourselves and not for the person we are forgiving.

If you ask me, I believe in second chances now more than ever, but not in third chances. This does not mean that someone accidentally repeating the offence automatically counts as the third fault. I am aware that while redeeming themselves, a person might fall back a bit into their old ways. That is okay as long as the guilt is genuine and the drive for redemption is still there. Genuineness, in terms of forgiveness, is the main aspect, and how you see or measure that genuineness is up to you. There is no machine which can calculate it for you.

Well, what do we even get from forgiveness? And I do not mean just us, but anyone around us, including the person we are forgiving. For starters, forgiveness starts relaxing that distrustful mindset which slowly leaks into everything. It begins to consume you, rot you and make you bitter, due to which it agonises you and the people you love somewhere along the way.

In Ted Lasso Season 3, in the episode called Mom City, Jamie Tartt keeps looking into the stands during a match. Ted asks him why he keeps doing that and what is there. Jamie says he is checking whether his father has shown up, and that bothers him because he hates his father. He also mentions that much of his hunger for football came from spite for his dad, and for some reason that hunger is not working anymore.

Ted suggests that if hating his father is not doing its thing anymore, then maybe Jamie should try something different, which is forgiving him. Jamie scoffs and says he ain’t giving his father that relief. Ted then tells him: “You ain’t giving him anything. When you choose to do that, you’re giving that to yourself.”

It hit me at that moment that forgiveness is first and foremost for yourself, for the baggage you are carrying and for all the anger you have suppressed somewhere inside. Jamie’s father is not even in the stands, but Jamie keeps looking for him. The man does not have to be present to affect him anymore. Jamie thinks forgiveness would free his father from something, while it is Jamie who needs to be freed from it. So I guess sometimes the forgiver and the forgivee are the same person, hehe.

But of course, if they are not the same, the forgivee, if forgiven and genuinely sorry, can turn their life around. Rebecca in Season 1 is a good example of that. She causes massive problems for Ted and tries to sabotage him behind his back out of pure spite and heartbreak over her divorce. She is basically using her own trauma to tear down a guy who has only brought kindness into her life.

When Rebecca finally tells Ted what she has done, he could have easily hated her for it. Instead, he looks past her actions and sees the pain behind them when he tells her: “Divorce is hard. It hits everybody different.” Rebecca was already guilty and came clean on her own. Ted’s forgiveness worked because she wanted to stop being that person. If she did not care about what she had done, the same forgiveness would probably have meant nothing. This is again where genuine guilt comes into the picture.

Now, concluding with an open note for you, in case you have not yet been convinced about forgiving that ex or that childhood friend with whom you fought five years ago. We are all sinners, we all make mistakes, and we are just an ever learning ball of emotions who somehow figured out how to make a rock think by making chips from silica rocks.

Quoting Ted Lasso again, because yeah, I know, it is my favourite show: “I hope that either all of us, or none of us, are judged by the actions of our weakest moments, but rather by the strength we show when and if we’re ever given a second chance.”

posts.title: You Cannot Defeat a Person Who Is Having Fun
posts.description: A very non-literal psychological essay on finding your best self.
posts.html:
I was worried when I turned 25 that my life was amounting to nothing and that I had done something wrong or missed big opportunities, but looking back now, I realize my only crime is that I am in my 20s. There is nothing that can be done, and this is the time to feel all of this. In this generation of constant competition and super-awareness of who is doing what, the critic becoming worse and controlling you is likely.

And yet, I think a lot about how we all have a critic and we simply never realize how toxic it eventually becomes. All of our insecurities, negative emotions, and fears of being judged come from that entity. For most, it operates in a very simple way: a negative comment from an external entity is noted, while an active compliment is forgotten. The critic is the reason you don’t feel good about a compliment, but criticism is taken to heart.

To understand why, I have thought long and really hard about it (I know what you are going to say), and I realized that there are various personas of ourselves. I am not talking about the ones we show to others. These are inner angels and demons. There is a part that is developed when we live our teenage years until we get out of college. Think of the teenage one as having high energy to execute but low capability to make smart decisions. The teen version comes out when you are in a new environment, maybe? Or, basically, when you try uncharted territories or simply go into survival mode.

Then, there is an adult version of us that is developed to accommodate this new life post-academics. This guy thinks more and does less, with high thinking capability but low execution energy. Then, there is you, who eventually becomes conscious of both of them. The ‘You’ who is able to see both of these versions is an observer and the real consciousness behind ‘You’. Technically, it is also YOU. In psychology, these are called the ‘id’ (the teen), the ‘superego’ (the adult), and the ‘ego’ (the observer).

Internally, I feel the critic—which acts as the toxic ‘superego’—usually attacks the ‘id’ because it is more vulnerable. The conscious observer, your ‘ego’, is honestly a good alternative to the critic, and you should try to replace it with it. Note down how the critic fools you, manipulates you, and puts unbearable expectations on you. Try to reason with them as an adult, and then you might be ready to battle your critic better. Eventually, you realize that this isn’t you anymore, but you did it; you feel like you are going back to your old habits and ways, which might seem depressing or good depending on how you perceive that. You definitely question it.

The real solution, and my real point for writing this article, was exactly this: how to understand what is going on, figure out the solution, and become a kid again when it comes to achieving something. I forgot to add that there is an extension to the teen called ‘the kid’ (not a psychological ontology). This guy is awesome; he does everything just for the fun of it.

For me, I used to use hate from the critic on my teen to get things done; it was a great motivator, but really bad for the long term. Burnout was imminent. I was complaining that I was doing everything that I wanted, but I didn’t feel satisfied even though I was doing everything my way. There was a lingering part that was performing for the audience. Eventually, I took breaks—major ones—from things I was great at. But now that I see it, I want to do all those things again, not for the audience, or power, or fame, but for the fun of it. You cannot reason with or defeat a person who is having fun.

When you reach this point, there is a certain comfort because there is no show going on anymore, no performance to be led, just a life to be lived. There are days and moments when I am so genuine to myself that it makes me feel lucky to be alive, like the movie ‘Soul’. I feel that even though I might not become someone, at least my life will be more happily fulfilled than forced or rushed. It is 100% a privilege, but what isn’t? Am I right? Although, I am recognizing it more and more with gratitude.

Being alone and doing things alone (not being lonely) will open you to thoughts you won’t believe you were capable of thinking. Also, all in all, life works out, so it is better to live it than worry too much about it. You are such a beautiful human being; give yourself some grace. :)

posts.title: how to start enjoying life as it was intended
posts.html:
So, it’s been established by the fact that if you are reading this, you somewhere believe that the progress of humanity has been pointing towards a bit of a wrong direction. And everybody is becoming a bit more unhappy with their lives, like feeling a void, and once that void is filled, racing towards filling the next one. You see the pattern here. RAT RACE.

We know what should be done (deep down for sure) but no one is willing to do it. You are not alone, nor a culprit of the whole issue. You are not as lazy as you think you are. You are in fact much smarter than you think. How do I know this? Well, for the fact that the internet bombarded us with information, and initially it was great. People were getting more and more aware, but eventually, that’s all they started to do. CONSUME.

Soon the dopamine that consumption gave us started to feel stale, so we were moved on to platforms where they competed for our attention. We became livestock for them to suck the thinking and creativity out of. So yeah, you aren’t as dumb or lazy as you think you are.

Coming to what this piece of “Writing” is all about: how to start enjoying life as it was intended. Honestly, I want to make you believe how good life is when rejecting modernity and accepting analog, or basically finding a balance between productivity and enjoying life. I feel the way it is, is that we all have some forced ill habits that make us miserable. I know for sure I do; for me, it is doomscrolling.

Even if I remove my access to Instagram, I will start scrolling YouTube Shorts or any other short videos, because every place is now filled with such a pattern.

The problem is not even an app anymore; it’s a hunger for dopamine and like an addiction, of course. Along with that, there are too many marketing notifications to grab your attention, lighting up your phone, making us wonder if it’s an important notification. By the way, if you read this far, you have the capability to escape from this dystopia.

So, I wanted to block out YouTube Shorts without blocking out YouTube, as I use it for music, etc. I came across an app which specifically does that (only Android ☹️) called minimal launcher. But even with that blocked, I realized that whenever I wanted to record myself thinking, I needed to keep opening my phone. It was so inconvenient and distracting to have that screen back in my face, so the urge to get a digicam occurred.

Then I realized, what if I go full analog?

Get the physical thing for everything, just as it was before the smartphone era, as it was supposed to be. Now, on why I wanted to record myself: it was so that I can hear my thoughts out loud, as journaling isn’t always convenient. I have always done a lot of brain dumps, but scrawling on a small copy doesn’t always cut it when your thoughts are way too interconnected and complex. So I got a whiteboard. Big thoughts need big places to scrawl.

Regardless, all of these are OK, but how do you even get the patience for it? Well, get bored. That’s it—get freaking bored. Don’t do anything for a good amount of time, just sit and try to keep yourself awake. If you sleep, you kinda forfeit and start from the beginning when you wake up. I mean, try not to nod off. It will feel like a waste of time, but trust me, it’s not.

And once you feel like you can’t do it anymore, start consuming a ~1-hour episode of a show or something—anything above 40 minutes—to give yourself a reward. Consumption is not all bad, but there should be a limit to it. The easier it is to get to the bottom line faster and faster, the more the value of the journey diminishes. As you get into quick iterations, it becomes an unintentional habit; you forget you are even doing it.

Once you are able to get bored, creativity starts flowing, and once that happens, you should pour it out however you want, regardless of the type or quality. If you wanna sketch, just doodle it. Write minor labels explaining things if the worst-case scenario is that your doodle is illegibly bad. The point is to exercise your brain. Record, photograph, edit, canvas it, do whatever engages your creativity. Write down what you are able to and double down. Art is an expression of one’s unexplainable self, and to quantize art into monetary value alone is a crime.

So, the distribution of each work and tool makes you more intentional with that work. A vlog from a phone might be a bit more distracting than a digicam. So pick analog tools more, as they are more intentional. Don’t start or buy them right away; see if what I am saying applies to you or not. Are you distracted by other things when using those features from your phone? Start keeping a sling or small bag to keep your stuff with you, as analog items don’t usually fit in pockets. Spend time alone and you will find how important these tools are to you as an individual.

All of the above has been for making yourself intentional and confident in yourself, and becoming more aware as a self-healing feedback loop [reference the wiki page for system theory feedback loop]. Now, how do you make more genuine, positive relations with people? Such that you keep your environment positive and healthy so it doesn’t worsen your own feedback cycle.

Well, for existing people in your life—the good, the bad, and the ugly—start picking each one and seeing them as humans. Not anything else, just plain and simple humans. Once you are able to establish that, you can choose which ones are worth enough for your energy and their sincerity to become more open and genuine with. Understand their love language and try to replicate it every fortnight, or however you feel is suitable. These days, we have a habit of simply interjecting ourselves into an incident or convo that the other person is trying to convey. In my opinion, focus on the other person fully when they are telling you something. Ask questions. Listen to listen, not to think of a reply.

When it comes to strangers, just start a conversation genuinely. Don’t overthink it—be casual about it. Say hi, notice something about them, and if the conversation naturally drops, let it drop. You don’t have to force yourself to keep it going.

Every moment you slow your brain, you are healing yourself, like a poison leaving your body.

All in all, heal, so you might realize just how much less miserable your life can be, and how smart you actually are. Clear the noise, and see things clearly.

Things to do instead of doomscrolling:

  • Keep a mini diary.

    • Write your favorites lists, like moments in a sitcom, types of niche mistakes of your hobby, etc.

    • Write about what people in your circle like, dislike, love language, best moments with them, etc

  • Get into a habit or hobby of collecting something nicher everytime of a particular genre.

  • Go out and try to create a story for any person you see on the road, try to give it as much depth as you can, after you do, see what does the story contain the visuals from? empathy? anger? jealousy? that is a good way of understanding your emotions as well.
